patterns.name: Present tense: verbs end in -r
patterns.explain_en: Swedish verbs in the present tense usually end in -r: talar, bor, läser, går. The form is the same for every person: jag bor, du bor, hon bor, vi bor.

patterns.name: My and your: min, mitt, mina
patterns.explain_en: Words like "my" change to match the noun: min with en-words (min bil), mitt with ett-words (mitt hus) and mina in the plural (mina barn). Din, ditt, dina ("your") and vår, vårt, våra ("our") work the same way.

patterns.name: Verb second: I dag regnar det
patterns.explain_en: In a Swedish statement the verb is always the second part. So when a sentence starts with a time or a place, the subject moves after the verb: I dag regnar det, not "I dag det regnar".

patterns.name: Particle verbs: tycka om, komma ihåg, ge upp
patterns.explain_en: Many verbs have a small stressed word, a particle, that changes the meaning: tycka om (like), komma ihåg (remember), hälsa på (visit), ge upp (give up). The particle follows the verb, after the subject if that comes after the verb, and it carries the stress.

patterns.explain_en: In a Swedish statement the verb is always the second part. So when a sentence starts with a time or a place, the subject moves after the verb: I dag regnar det, not "I dag det regnar".

patterns.name: My and your: min, mitt, mina
patterns.explain_en: Words like "my" change to match the noun: min with en-words (min bil), mitt with ett-words (mitt hus) and mina in the plural (mina barn). Din, ditt, dina ("your") and vår, vårt, våra ("our") work the same way.

patterns.name: Comparing: större, störst and mer, mest
patterns.explain_en: Most adjectives add -are and -ast to compare: billig, billigare, billigast. Some change more (stor, större, störst; bra, bättre, bäst), and many long words use mer and mest: mer spännande. "Than" is än.

patterns.name: Questions: the verb comes first
patterns.explain_en: In a yes/no question the verb comes first: Bor du här? In a question with a question word (vad, var, när, hur, vem) the verb comes right after that word: Var bor du?

patterns.name: Not: inte comes after the verb
patterns.explain_en: To say "not", put inte after the verb: Jag dricker inte kaffe. Swedish needs no helper like English "do". If the subject comes after the verb, inte comes after the subject: I dag arbetar jag inte.

patterns.name: Past tense: -ade, -de, -te and strong verbs
patterns.explain_en: The past tense is the same for every person. Regular verbs end in -ade, -de or -te (pratade, stängde, köpte); strong verbs change their vowel instead (gick, åt, drack, var).

patterns.name: Commands: the verb stem (Ta! Kom! Sätt dig!)
patterns.explain_en: A command uses the verb without -r, the same as the infinitive without its -a ending if it has one: Ta en kaka! Sätt dig! Glöm inte nyckeln!
patterns.level_reason: Built from the infinitive, which the ladder brings in at A2 with modal verbs (G-A2-04).

patterns.name: Reflexive verbs: tvätta sig, känna sig
patterns.explain_en: Some verbs take a pronoun that points back to the subject: jag tvättar mig, du tvättar dig, hon tvättar sig, vi tvättar oss. Sig is for han, hon, den, det and de. Often English has no "self": känna sig means "feel".

patterns.name: There is: det finns
patterns.explain_en: Swedish says "there is" or "there are" with det finns (det fanns in the past): Det finns en park här. The thing that exists comes after finns.
patterns.level_reason: A fixed everyday chunk met from the first texts, like the A1 present tense (G-A1-01) it is built on.

patterns.name: Particle verbs: tycka om, komma ihåg, ge upp
patterns.explain_en: Many verbs have a small stressed word, a particle, that changes the meaning: tycka om (like), komma ihåg (remember), hälsa på (visit), ge upp (give up). The particle follows the verb, after the subject if that comes after the verb, and it carries the stress.
